Fig. 2. Changes in nutrient concentrations (soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP), NO\(_x^-\)-N and NH\(_4^+\)) (\(\mu\)g L\(^{-1}\)) of tidal water as it flooded the cyanobacterial mat at Giralia Bay, Exmouth Gulf, Western Australia, during three tidal cycles.

Results

Nutrient exchange during tidal inundation

During field experiments, concentrations of NO\(_x^-\)-N and NH\(_4^+\) decreased as the tidal cycle progressed (Fig. 2). The decrease in NO\(_x^-\)-N was pronounced, with concentrations almost halved as the tidal cycle progressed, with a rate of \(-1.3 \pm 0.58\) \(\mu\)g L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\) and a decrease in concentration from 15 \(\mu\)g L\(^{-1}\) at the beginning of the flood tide to \(\sim 7\) \(\mu\)g L\(^{-1}\) at the end of the ebb tide. The regression for NO\(_x^-\)-N decrease over time was significant (\(R^2 = 0.39\), \(F_{1,10} = 6.27\), \(P = 0.031\)). Concentrations of NH\(_4^+\) also decreased over a tidal cycle, although clearly only during one tidal cycle, when concentrations decreased from 60 \(\mu\)g L\(^{-1}\) at the beginning of the flood to \(\sim 30\) \(\mu\)g L\(^{-1}\) on the ebb tide, with a rate of \(-6.8\) \(\mu\)g L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\). The concentrations of SRP throughout a tidal cycle were more variable, increasing in some tidal cycles and decreasing in others (Fig. 2). Overall, during our field experiments, the cyanobacterial mat removed nutrients from the floodwater, contrary to our first hypothesis (H1), which predicted that nutrients were released to the floodwater during tidal inundation.

Nutrient exchange in chambers

In the nutrient-chamber experiments, we observed results similar to those of the field experiments. During the experiment, NO\(_x^-\)-N concentrations decreased in the chambers with cyanobacterial mat, whereas NH\(_4^+\) concentrations decreased not only in the chambers with cyanobacterial mat but also in the chambers with sediment only. Concentrations of SRP did not significantly change during our experiments. The removal of NO\(_x^-\)-N and NH\(_4^+\) by the cyanobacterial mat occurred only in light conditions. Sediment without mat removed NH\(_4^+\) during dark conditions (Fig. 3, Table 1). The chamber experiments provided evidence that supports our second hypothesis (H2) that nutrient exchange in cyanobacterial mats is higher in the day than at night.

When comparing desiccated and wet cyanobacterial mats, concentrations of NO\(_x^-\)-N, NH\(_4^+\) and SRP decreased in both treatments as soon as the experiment started (Fig. 4, Table 1). All the regressions for the removal of nutrients over time in this experiment were significant (\(P < 0.01\)) (Table 1). There was no difference between the nutrient exchange of the wet and the desiccated cyanobacterial mats. Thus, regardless of previous desiccation, the cyanobacterial mat removed nutrients from the floodwater during tidal inundation.

In general, nutrient concentrations in the blank samples (containing only filtered seawater) did not change considerably during the course of the experiments. However, in the last experiment (desiccated v. wet, Fig. 4), the NH\(_4^+\) concentration decreased in the control chamber, in addition to declines observed in the chambers with cyanobacterial mat. Furthermore, during the experiments conducted in the light, the initial NO\(_x^-\)-N concentrations in the blank chamber were much lower than those in the chambers with the cyanobacterial mat and sediment only, which suggests a release of NO\(_x^-\)-N to the water column as soon as the cyanobacterial mat and sediment chambers were flooded (Figs 3, 4).

Nitrogen fixation

The mean N fixation rate was \(1.7 \pm 0.26\) nmol N cm\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\) (\(4.9 \pm 0.77\) nmol C\(_2\)H\(_2\) N cm\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\)). In comparison, the removal of N from the floodwater was 3.2 nmol N cm\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\). Thus, N fixation accounts for 34% of total N incorporation, a result that supports our third hypothesis that N fixation is a significant component of N incorporation into the cyanobacterial mat. N-fixation rates were higher during the day (\(2.7 \pm 0.36\) nmol N cm\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\); \(8.0 \pm 1.1\) nmol C\(_2\) H\(_2\) N cm\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\)) than at night (\(1.1 \pm 0.34\) nmol N cm\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\); \(3.2 \pm 1.0\) nmol C\(_2\) H\(_2\) N cm\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\)) (\(F_{1,9} = 19.2\), \(P = 0.002\)) (Table 2), a result that rejects our fourth hypothesis (H4). N-fixation rates in the lower intertidal zone were higher than those in the higher intertidal zone (\(F_{1,4} = 11.1\), \(P = 0.03\)), supporting our fifth hypothesis (H5).

High N-removal rates from the floodwater occurred mainly under light conditions, a result that confirms our second hypothesis (H2). Removal of nutrients under light conditions is likely to be a result of higher activity and metabolic demands of the mat during the day. Light and dark comparisons may have been confounded by differences in nutrient concentrations of the seawater used for each experiment because of nutrient pulses associated with the approaching cyclone, which may affect nutrient assimilation (Saunders and Kalff 2001). However, similar results of cyanobacterial mat assimilating N (NO\(_3^-\) and NH\(_4^+\)) at greater rates in light than in dark conditions have previously been reported in temperate cyanobacterial mats in Georgia, USA (Porubsky et al. 2008). Cyanobacterial mat composition Our visual observations of the mat community showed that the cyanobacterial mat in the Exmouth Gulf is composed mainly of sheaths, probably derived from species from the Oscillatoriales. Sheaths of cyanobacteria generally preserve well compared with other structures (Bartley 1996), which explains their abundance and high contribution to the structure of the mat. Fig. 5. There was a clear difference in the morphology of the living cells from the high and low intertidal samples. Although we found Microcoleus sp. in both the low and high intertidal zones, the low intertidal-zone samples had abundant coccoid cells, whereas the high intertidal-zone samples had abundant filamentous forms. The cyanobacterial 16s rDNA analysis confirmed the identity and presence of M. chthonoplastes. Low intertidal-zone samples also had Oscillatoria spp. Two bands were also observed that did not show high homology with other published cyanobacterial sequences. Our results provided some evidence that differing communities, or at least morphologies, of cyanobacteria are found across the intertidal zone (H6).

The cyanobacteria composition described in the present study is similar to that in the north-western Dampier Archipelago (200 km north), where Microcoleus chthonoplastes and Geitlerniema sp. (previously Phormidium sp.) were also found (Paling et al. 1989). Our study adds to this species list of cyanobacteria in these arid-zone estuaries, with the occurrence of Plectonema sp., Leptolyngbya sp. and Lyngbya aestuarii in the high intertidal-zone samples.

Nitrogen fixation
The mean N fixation was 1.7 ± 0.33 nmol N cm⁻² h⁻¹, accounting for 34% of total N incorporated by the cyanobacterial mat (N fixation plus N removal during tidal inundation). This result confirms that N fixation is an important mechanism for N incorporation by the cyanobacterial mat in this region (H3). It is probable that N fixation is performed by Oscillatoria sp., Plectonema sp., Leptolyngbya sp., Lyngbya aestuarii, Geitlerniema sp. and Microcoleus. However, Leptolyngbya can fix N only if associated with heterotrophic bacteria (Li et al. 2010).

Our results indicated that cyanobacterial mats in Exmouth Gulf are capable of fixing N during the day and at night, with higher rates during the day. Thus, our hypothesis that N-fixation rates were highest at night (H4) was rejected. Diurnal N fixation would suggest the presence of heterocystous cells because of the fact that N fixation is very sensitive to oxygen, which is produced during photosynthesis. However, the species we found in the mat are non-heterocystous forms. Nevertheless, some species of non-heterocystous cyanobacteria have alternative mechanisms that allow them to fix N during both night and day, in both anaerobic and aerobic conditions. Such mechanisms include microanaerobiosis (e.g. Plectonema; Berman-Frank et al. 2003), cellular differentiation (e.g. Trichodesmus; Berman-Frank et al. 2003) or intracellular processes still to be understood (e.g. Lyngbya; Jones 1992), such as inclusion granules (Cyanothece; Reddy et al. 1993). Some species of Plectonema that lack heterocysts have been observed to require light to fix N (Misra and Rakesh 1994). Thus, the occurrence of Plectonema and Lyngbya in the high intertidal zone suggest that these species may be responsible for diurnal N fixation.

As hypothesised (H5), the cyanobacterial mat from the low intertidal zone had higher N-fixation rates than did the cyanobacterial mat at higher intertidal elevations. These results indicated that the biogeochemical function of the cyanobacterial mat varies over the intertidal zone. The difference in N-fixation rates between the low and high intertidal zones could be related to lower salinities and more frequent tidal flushing in the low intertidal zone, which favour N fixation (Paling et al. 1989; Toledo et al. 1995; Kyaruzi et al. 2003). Differences in N fixation between cyanobacterial mats from the low and high intertidal zones might also be a consequence of different cyanobacterial community compositions along the desiccation gradient, as has been observed in a subtropical arid wetland in Baja California Sur, Mexico (Rothrock and Garcia-Pichel 2005) and is suggested in the present study. Variation in N-fixation rates over tidal elevation has also been reported for an intertidal bank in the Wadden Sea (Severin and Stal 2008).

Our results showed that N fixation is temporally and spatially variable and suggested a significant role of N fixation in this ecosystem. The N-fixation rates we measured in our study site (ranging from 1.4 to 8.2 nmol C₂ H₂ cm⁻² h⁻¹, mean 4.9 ± 0.77 nmol C₂ H₂ cm⁻² h⁻¹) were similar to those in cyanobacterial mats in Dampier, Western Australia (0.8–6 nmol C₂ H₂ cm⁻² h⁻¹; Paling et al. 1989), lower than those found in intertidal mudflats in California, USA (37 nmol C₂H₂ cm⁻² h⁻¹; Joye and Paerl 1994), within the range of those found in the intertidal zone of the lagoon of Aladabra Atoll (0.6–125 nmol C₂ H₂ cm⁻² h⁻¹; Potts and Whitton 1977) and higher than those measured in mangrove sediments in Zanzibar (0.001 nmol C₂ H₂ cm⁻² h⁻¹; Kyaruzi et al. 2003). Thus, N fixation at our study site could be considerable, especially because of the large areas (>100 km²) occupied by cyanobacterial mats in this region.

The results from the present study have provided insights into the role of cyanobacterial mats in nutrient exchange in coastal arid wetlands during periods of rainfall. The conditions in which we conducted our experiment were very different from conditions that occur most frequently in the region because of the increase in nutrients associated with the rain brought by Cyclone Pancho. The rain and flooding could have strongly modified the nutrient exchange of the cyanobacterial mat. For example, although the N-fixation rates measured were very similar to those measured by Paling et al. (1989), they are likely to be underestimated, as the increased N input resulting from runoff during the tropical cyclone reduces N-fixation rates (Joye and Paerl 1993). Nutrient assimilation during tidal exchange may have also been particularly high during the sampling period because an increase in nutrients enhances assimilation (Joye and Paerl 1993). Thus, the contribution of N fixation to total N incorporation under normal conditions could be higher than the one reported in the present study. Furthermore, the acetylene–ethylene method used to measure N fixation has some limitations, including (1) the relatively long time required to achieve a high, stable ethylene production, (2) the inhibition of acetylene reduction at high acetylene partial pressures and (3) incomplete saturation sites for ethylene production at low partial pressures (Patriquin and Denike 1978). The acetylene–ethylene reduction method can also overestimate N-fixation rates because it measures gross N fixation, without taking into account N loss by other processes such as denitrification (Howarth et al. 1988; Mahaffey et al. 2005). Although we maintained standard conditions between runs (6 h, 25°C), adding confidence to our relative comparisons (low v. high in the intertidal; day v. night), there is potential for error in our comparison of N fixation with N incorporation during tidal inundation. munities under study. The chambers were allowed to adjust to their new light regime for 15–20 min prior to the initiation of the acetylene reduction assays. The amount of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) received by the algal communities within each chamber was calculated from in situ light readings, combined with the percentage of transmission through each screen, calculated by use of a LICOR LI-1800 Spectroradiometer within a tub of lake water under low wave conditions. The in situ light readings were taken concurrent to, and directly beside, the acetylene reduction assays by use of a LICOR LI-1000 Data Logger and Quantum Sensor with a flat plate collector. Algal collection, heterocyst enumeration, and chlorophyll—After most experiments, duplicate or triplicate algal samples were taken from the rock surface within each chamber by use of a periphyton-scraping device, as described by Loeb (1981). The periphyton samples were stored in the dark and returned to the laboratory, where subsamples were taken for chlorophyll a analysis and heterocyst enumeration. Chl a was extracted from filtered subsamples at −5°C for ~14 h by use of an alkaline acetone solution, according to the methods of Stainton et al. (1977), and analyzed fluorometrically. For each site and depth combination, five algal samples were randomly chosen for heterocyst enumeration. A 2-ml subsample was placed in a Utermöhl chamber, and at least 50 fields (or 100 heterocysts) were counted by use of a Zeiss Axioinvert 35 inverted phase microscope with 400× magnification. Each sample to be counted was selected randomly, such that the person counting did not know the site or depth from which it originated. Daytime N₂ fixation—During daylight hours, rates of nitrogen fixation were easily detectable in all transparent chambers (Table 1), whereas rates in opaque chambers were typically 4%–7% of rates in transparent chambers, which indicates that photosynthetic cyanoprokaryotes were responsible for the majority N₂ fixation rates noted. The dominance of heterocystous forms of Calothrix at virtually all sites and depths studied (Higgins 1999) make it highly probable that they were responsible for the majority of daytime N₂ fixation by the periphyton community. Cyanoprokaryotic endosymbionts capable of N₂ fixation were found in several species of the diatom Rhopalodia; however, their total biovolume was generally an order of magnitude less than Calothrix heterocyst biovolume (Higgins 1999); therefore, they likely do not contribute largely to the overall fixation rates noted. The range of daytime N₂ fixation rates was 1–2,920 \( \mu \)g N m⁻² h⁻¹, with variability generally <30% of the mean value for each site/depth (Table 1). The Maleri Island sites, which are known to be impacted annually by a plume of sediment- and nutrient-rich water extending from the nearby Linthipe River (Bootsma and Hecky 1999), are an exception and have much higher variability, especially at 10 m depth. At the Maleri South site, a 1–2 cm layer of silt covering rocky surfaces was noted below 7 m depth, and rocky surfaces had a relatively low total standing crop of periphyton and biovolume of heterocysts (Higgins 1999). Nitrogen fixation, Chl a, and heterocyst biovolume—Of the parameters known to influence N₂ fixation, the strongest correlation was found with heterocyst biovolume (\( R = 0.71, P < 0.005 \); Fig. 1) and solar insolation (discussed below). Both N₂ fixation rates and heterocyst biovolume showed generally decreasing values with increasing depth at all sites sampled (Fig. 2a–e, Table 1). In contrast to studies on the epilithic periphyton of five northern temperate lakes by Loeb and Reuter (1981), chlorophyll and N₂ fixation were not highly correlated in the epilithic periphyton of Lake Malawi (\( R = 0.04, P = 0.70 \)). Studies on coral reefs have shown an inverse relationship between N₂ fixation and chlorophyll, which was attributed to the grazing activity of fish keeping the periphyton community in an early succesional stage, decreasing chlorophyll concentrations while increasing rates of primary production and nitrogen fixation (Wilkinson and Sammarco 1983; Larkum 1988). This simulation predicts that the maximum difference in nitrogen fixation rates due to seasonal differences in solar radiation is ~15% of the annual mean value. The 1 June 1997 simulation was also used to compare model estimates with in situ estimates of hourly N_2 fixation at midday for 2, 5, and 10 m depths (Table 1, Fig. 2f). The 1 June 1997 simulation for 2 m depth predicted a N_2 fixation rate of 1,490 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}, which fell within the range of N_2 fixation rates for each site, with the exception of LI-Makalawe and Thumbi West (Table 1, Fig. 2f) and agreed with the site-averaged in situ N_2 fixation rate of 1,500 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}. The model predicted values of 910 and 370 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1} for 5 and 10 m depths, which agreed closely with the site-averaged in situ estimates of 950 and 410 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}. Patch-specific and nocturnal rates of nitrogen fixation— Above 1 m depth at all sites, and from 0–5 m depth at Maleri South, visually distinct patches of epilithic periphyton dominated by Calothrix or Cladophora were observed throughout the sampling season (May–October). At other sites and depths, the epilithic periphyton community was more homogenous and was dominated by heterocystous Calothrix spp (Higgins 1999; Higgins unpubl. data). The biomass of Calothrix patches were dominated by heterocystous Calothrix species, whereas the biomass of Cladophora patches were codominated by Cladophora, Calothrix, and a variety of epiphytic diatoms (Higgins 1999). Calothrix patches at 2 m depth had significantly higher rates of nitrogen fixation (1,450 ± 540 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}; \( X \pm SD; n = 6 \)) than Cladophora patches (720 ± 90 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}, \( X \pm SD; n = 6 \)) during daylight hours (\( t \)-test, \( P = 0.03 \)). The relative patchiness in the epilithic periphyton community structure at shallow depths of the Maleri Island sites is likely responsible for the higher variability in N_2 fixation rates noted (Table 1), whereas the impacts of sediment accumulation account for the high variability at deeper depths. The mean rate of nocturnal nitrogen fixation in Calothrix patches, from 1–2 m depth, was double that for Cladophora patches, was ~60% of the daytime averages for nitrogen fixation (Tables 1, 2), and was an order of magnitude larger than rates measured in opaque chambers during the day. Although the difference in N_2 fixation rates between daytime dark box and nocturnal dark box experiments was unexpected, there are a number of plausible explanations. First, nocturnal N_2 fixation by nonheterocystous diazotrophs might occur primarily at night, when O_2 inhibition is reduced (i.e., the temporal separation of N_2 fixation and O_2 evolution processes). Second, the length of incubation during daytime dark box experiments may have been insufficient to allow a shift in adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and reductant pathways, which differ between day and night within heterocystous diazotrophs (Stewart 1973). The agreement between model estimates and in situ estimates for N₂ fixation allowed us to estimate daytime N₂ fixation throughout the littoral zone. From a maximal carbon fixation rate of 1 g m⁻² d⁻¹ (Bootsma 1993) and a “Redfield” C : N ratio of 5.68 (molar), the calculated 24-h N demand of periphyton would be 170 mg N m⁻² d⁻¹. From model estimates of daily N₂ fixation at shallow depths (1–2 m), N₂ fixation would contribute between 8% and 12% of the total 24-hr N demand of epilithic periphyton and between 13% and 18% if nocturnal N₂ fixation were included. To estimate the importance of epilithic N₂ fixation to the N budget of Lake Malawi, we employed our model to spatially and temporally integrate N₂ fixation rates over a depth gradient (under the assumption of a 45° slope) for a single year. Within the model, we multiplied area estimates over a range of factors (2–5.7), to adjust for roughness of the substrata (Higgins 1999), then extrapolated the results over the entire rocky littoral zone area in Lake Malawi, as determined from literature sources (Ribbink et al. 1983) and aerial surveys (Cooley unpubl. data). Although our model uses estimated daily PAR under 100% cloudless conditions from Fee’s (1990) model, we calculated depth-integrated rates under 70% cloudless conditions and found only a 10% difference in model output (due to light saturation at shallow depths). On the basis of these assumptions, the N₂ fixation model estimates that 4–20 × 10⁴ kg N lake⁻¹ yr⁻¹, or 40–120 mmol N m⁻² yr⁻¹, is biologically fixed by epilithic diazotrophs. This estimate for epilithic N₂ fixation is similar in magnitude to those for precipitation and riverine inputs to Lake Malawi and suggests that epilithic N₂ fixation may be a significant source of N to the epilimnion (Table 3). Furthermore, because epilithic N₂ fixation rates do not vary substantially between seasons, the relative importance of epilithic N₂ fixation increases during the dry-windy season, when riverine and atmospheric inputs of N and pelagic N₂ fixation are much reduced. Current remediation strategies of oiled ecosystems include application of nitrogen, or nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizers to oiled sediments [12, 13]. Increasing the supply of inorganic nutrients to sediments lowers the nutrient limitation of the hydrocarbonoclastic microbial community and leads to enhanced rates of hydrocarbon degradation. Optimizing the concentrations of pore water inorganic nutrients by application of fertilizers that result in the greatest hydrocarbon degradation, however, remains challenging [14, 42]. This data suggests that while additional input of oil at a site with a prior history of contamination does not lead to increased denitrification; however, denitrification increases substantially in response to higher nitrate availability. Therefore, if the remediation of a chronically oiled site relies on the application of fertilizers, monitoring pore water nitrate availability will be necessary to ensure that concentrations are maintained at levels that are adequate for optimal hydrocarbon degradation. Significant nonsymbiotic nitrogen fixation in Patagonian ombrotrophic bogs

KLAUS-HOLGER KNORR1, MARCUS A. HORN2 and WERNER BORKEN3
1Institute for Landscape Ecology, Hydrology Group, University of Münster, Heisenbergstr. 2, 48149 Münster, Germany,
2Department of Ecological Microbiology, University of Bayreuth, Dr.-Hans-Frisch-Str. 1-3, 95448 Bayreuth, Germany,
3Department of Soil Ecology, University of Bayreuth, Dr.-Hans-Frisch-Str. 1-3, 95448 Bayreuth, Germany

Abstract

Nitrogen (N) nutrition in pristine peatlands relies on the natural input of inorganic N through atmospheric deposition or biological dinitrogen (N2) fixation. However, N2 fixation and its significance for N cycling, plant productivity, and peat buildup are mostly associated with the presence of Sphagnum mosses. Here, we report high nonsymbiotic N2-fixation rates in two pristine Patagonian bogs with diversified vegetation and natural N deposition. Nonsymbiotic N2 fixation was measured in samples from 0 to 10, 10 to 20, and 40 to 50 cm depth using the 15N2 assay as well as the acetylene reduction assay (ARA). The ARA considerably underestimated N2 fixation and can thus not be recommended for peatland studies. Based on the 15N2 assay, high nonsymbiotic N2-fixation rates of 0.3–1.4 μmol N2 g−1 day−1 were found down to 50 cm under micro-oxic conditions (2 vol.%) in samples from plots covered by Sphagnum magellanicum or by vascular cushion plants, latter characterized by dense and deep aerenchyma roots. Peat N concentrations point to greater potential of nonsymbiotic N2 fixation under cushion plants, likely because of the availability of easily decomposable organic compounds and oxic conditions in the rhizosphere. In the Sphagnum plots, high N2 fixation below 10 cm depth rather reflects the potential during dry periods or low water level when oxygen penetrates the top peat layer and triggers peat mineralization. Natural abundance of the 15N isotope of live Sphagnum (5.6 δ‰) from 0 to 10 cm points to solely N uptake from atmospheric deposition and nonsymbiotic N2 fixation. A mean 15N signature of −0.7 δ‰ of peat from the cushion plant plots indicates additional N supply from N mineralization. Our findings suggest that nonsymbiotic N2 fixation overcomes N deficiency in different vegetation communities and has great significance for N cycling and peat accumulation in pristine peatlands.

Keywords: 15N, acetylen reduction assay, cushion plant, diazotroph, nitrogen cycle, nitrogen fixation, peatland, Sphagnum

Received 1 October 2014; revised version received 4 December 2014 and accepted 5 December 2014

Introduction

Peatlands store approximately 30% of the global soil organic carbon (C) mainly accumulated and preserved during the Holocene in the past 11 700 years (Gorham, 1991). Plant growth and peat accumulation rely on the permanent input of reactive nitrogen (N) as the recycling of organic N by mineralization is restricted by anoxic conditions in waterlogged peatlands. Natural N input by means of lightning of about 0.1 g m−2 yr−1 is an essential source of reactive N (Bragazza et al., 2005), but net accumulation rates of 0.2–0.5 g N m−2 yr−1 point to additional N sources (Loisel et al., 2014). Biological fixation of molecular nitrogen (N2) by symbiotic, associative, and free-living bacteria and archaea (diazotrophic organisms) is a widespread process that improves the N supply in N-limited ecosystems (Vitousek et al., 2013). It is generally thought that the potential of symbiotic N2 fixation is much greater than of associative and nonsymbiotic N2 fixation because of the high energy cost for enzymatic reduction of N2 to ammonia (NH3).

Indeed, peatlands inhabit only few plant species such as Myrica gale that host symbiotic N2-fixing bacteria in root nodules (Schwintzer, 1979). However, these symbiotic N2-fixing plant species do not exist in all peatlands or grow only in ecological niches. There are other non-nodule-forming plants which are associated with different groups of N2-fixing bacteria. N2-fixing heterocystous cyanobacteria are associated with Sphagnum mosses and increase the productivity of Sphagnum by higher N supply (Basilier et al., 1978). Recent studies indicate high N2 fixation by methanotrophic bacteria/archaea in or on the tissues of Sphagnum mosses (Bragina et al., 2013; Larmola et al., 2014). The N2-fixation rate is linked to oxidation of methane (CH4) as the main energy source (Larmola et al., 2014). From other ecosystems, it is known that different N2-fixing bacteria species live in the rhizosphere, as endophytes in intercellular spaces within live plant tissues or in intracellular spaces of dead plant cells (Franché et al., 2009). Results Variability in N content, N stocks, ¹⁵N signature, and C/N ratio N contents and N stocks generally increased with depth at both study sites (Table 1). Significant differences between the sites only occurred at 10–20 cm depth with higher N contents at SKY than at OBS (P = 0.01). CP plots had significantly higher N contents than the SPH plots at 0–10 cm (P < 0.001) and 10–20 cm depth (P = 0.018) while there was no vegetation effect at 40–50 cm depth. Interpolating the N stocks for the 20–40 cm peat layer resulted into total N stocks for the top 50 cm peat layer of 190–300 g m⁻². CP plots had 32% (OBS) and 59% (SKY) higher N stocks than the SPH plots. The molar C/N ratios ranged between 36 and 175 in the top 50 cm peat layer across both sites (Table 1). C/N ratios in the top 20 cm were smaller in the CP plots than in the SPH plots, but the differences at 40–50 cm were small between the vegetation types. Site had no effect on total P concentrations varying between 178 and 476 mg kg⁻¹ at the three depths. P concentrations decreased in the SPH plots and increased in the CP plots with depth. The δ¹⁵N signature increased with depth from −0.7 to 3.5‰ in the CP plots (Fig. 1). Opposite pattern revealed the SPH plots with a decrease from 6.4‰ at 0–10 cm to 1.4‰ at 40–50 cm depth. There was a significant site effect (OBS > SKY) on N₂ fixation at 10–20 cm (P < 0.001) and 40–50 cm (P < 0.001) depth and a significant vegetation effect (SPH > CP) for all depths (P < 0.003). The significant interaction (P = 0.004) of site and vegetation at 40–50 cm depth indicates that the site effect on N₂ fixation was different for SPH and CP. N₂-fixation rates varied from 27 to 216 mg N m⁻² day⁻¹ across both sites and all depths (Table 2). The rates were generally highest at 40–50 cm depth due to the greater peat density (0.06 g d.w. cm⁻³) compared to 0–10 and 10–20 cm depth (0.02–0.03 g d.w. cm⁻³).

Site had no effect on ethylene production at 0–10 and 10–20 cm depth, but the rate at 40–50 cm was significantly greater in OBS than in SKY (\( P < 0.001 \)). Vegetation had significant effects on ethylene production at 0–10 cm (\( P = 0.006 \)) and 10–20 cm (\( P = 0.004 \)) depth with higher rates in the CP plots than in the SPH plots. ANOVA revealed no interactions between the two factors site and vegetation. The mean ratio of ethylene production to \( ^{15}\mathrm{N}_2 \) uptake covered a wide span, ranging from 0.4 to 1.8 (Fig. 4). Ratios were smallest in the SPH plots, indicating a systematic vegetation effect on the ratio at 0–10 and 10–20 cm depth. In both vegetation types, the ratio decreased with increasing depth; whereby, the decline was stronger in the CP plots than in the SPH plots. At 40–50 cm depth, both vegetation types had similar ratios. Peat profile CH4 and DIC concentrations CH4 and DIC concentrations and vertical patterns differed between the SPH and CP plots at SKY (Fig. 5). In the SPH plot, CH4 linearly increased from almost atmospheric concentration at 0 cm depth to a maximum of about 160 \( \mu\mathrm{mol} \ \mathrm{L}^{-1} \) at 120 cm depth. In the CP plot, CH4 concentration was close to atmospheric concentration down to 100 cm depth, indicating the influence of aerenchymatic oxygen supply on CH4 turnover. Single aerenchymatic roots of A. pumila were found in peat cores from 50 to 100 cm depth although their influence on oxygenation and CH4 concentration at this depth is unclear. The effect of cushion plants on DIC concentrations was small. While DIC continuously increased with depth at the SPH plot, the maximum was reached in 80 cm depth at the CP plot. Discussion Nonsymbiotic \( \mathrm{N}_2 \) fixation in pristine peatlands Our results demonstrate the potential of nonsymbiotic \( \mathrm{N}_2 \) fixation in two ombrotrophic bogs of Patagonia. Together with recent findings from the northern hemisphere, it changes the prevailing view of insignificant nonsymbiotic \( \mathrm{N}_2 \) fixation and N deficiency in pristine peatlands. Likewise, a broader range of 0.5–6.2 g N m⁻² yr⁻¹ was attributed to CH₄-oxidizing bacteria in different Sphagnum species of boreal bogs (Vile et al., 2014). Basilier et al. (1978) already reported N₂-fixation rates of 0.5–6.4 g N m⁻² yr⁻¹ in the mire through an association of cyanobacteria with Sphagnum and Drepanocladus. In contrast, most of the earlier studies found rather small nonsymbiotic N₂-fixation rates in the range of <0.1–2.1 g N m⁻² yr⁻¹ (Waughman & Bellamy, 1980; Chapman & Hemond, 1982; Schwintzer, 1983). Our estimates of 63–78 mg N m⁻² day⁻¹ for the top 10 cm in living Sphagnum and peat under vascular plants exceed the average daily rates of other studies. Vile et al. (2014), for example, incubated only the top 5 cm of Sphagnum plots. We found, however, still live tissues of S. magellanicum at 10–20 cm depth and N₂ fixation even below that depth in peat from S. magellanicum. Another reason for our estimates being at the upper end is that the incubation temperature of 15 °C is higher than the mean temperature during growing season. Further, we assume that N₂ fixation in peatland was underestimated in some studies when ARA was used as solely method without calibration by the \(^{15}\)N₂ assay (see below). Therefore, we refer here to N₂-fixation rates determined with the \(^{15}\)N₂ assay.

The potential of nonsymbiotic N₂ fixation is hardly smaller in the peat layers below 10 cm depth, although we expect much smaller rates under in situ conditions. Disturbance of peat by sampling, root picking and thereby penetration of O₂ have likely triggered a sudden rise in the activity of heterotrophic diazotrophs. The adjusted O₂ concentration of about 2% during incubation was obviously sufficient for ongoing high activity of heterotrophic microorganisms. Similar conditions should irregularly arise in situ by water table fluctuations. Nonsymbiotic N₂ fixation could thus be stimulated in transient oxic peat layers during dry periods.

Most studies exclusively report on nonsymbiotic N₂ fixation in association with Sphagnum or other mosses (c.f. Basilier et al., 1978; Larmola et al., 2014; Vile et al., 2014). Slightly lower N₂-fixation rates under cushion plants in the absence of Sphagnum point to similar N availability in both vegetation types. In fact, we assume higher in situ rates under cushion plants for different reasons. First, the enormous biomass of aerenchyma roots acts as conduit for gas exchange between peat and the atmosphere in the top 50–100 cm of the peat. Redox potentials of >350 mV to a depth of 150 cm indicate the presence of O₂ in the rhizosphere of cushion plants while O₂ is almost absent in peat under Sphagnum (Fritz et al., 2011). Although O₂ profiles were not measured at our plots, low CH₄ concentrations down to 90 cm depth at the SKY-CP plot suggest thorough CH₄ oxidation in the rhizosphere at oxic conditions. Second, the cushion plants A. pumila and D. fascicularis release root exudates and produce relatively easily decomposable, barely lignified aerenchyma roots. We determined live root biomass of 0.9–1.1 kg d.w. m⁻² and estimated mean lifetimes of about 3–4 years using radiocarbon dating (data not shown), pointing to high root turnover.

Addition of root exudates or sugars induces a rapid increase in nonsymbiotic N₂ fixation (Bürgmann et al., 2005). An increase of N₂ fixation in two moss species also was achieved by long-term addition of birch litter (Sorensen & Michelsen, 2011), demonstrating the dependency of heterotrophic diazotrophs on C sources. Hence, the rhizosphere under cushion plants represents a favorable milieu for free-living diazotrophs.

Although the litter of Sphagnum is refractory and mainly contributes to peat accumulation (Bragazza et al., 2007), dissolved organic carbon (DOC) from Sphagnum leachates is easily biodegradable (Wickland et al., 2007). The increase in O₂ availability and consequent activation of oxygen-dependent enzymes like phenol oxidases (Freeman et al., 2004) in Sphagnum peat could have resulted into decomposition of both refractory organic compounds and DOC. Whether CH₄-oxidizing bacteria, the prevailing active diazotrophs in Sphagnum (Vile et al., 2014), or other diazotrophs were stimulated during sample processing remains unclear. Our apparent N₂-fixation rates for peat likely overestimated in situ conditions and rather demonstrate the potential of N₂ fixation at reduced water level.

Nitrogen status of ombrotrophic bogs

High apparent nonsymbiotic N₂-fixation rates suggest that N is a nonlimiting nutrient for plant growth in the studied peatlands, although N concentrations in the top 10 cm indicate small net N uptake and retention by vegetation. N fertilization did not affect biomass production, whereas the combined fertilization of N and P almost doubled biomass production of Sphagnum in a Patagonian bog (Fritz et al., 2012). Considering small P concentrations in the SPH and CP plots, P seems to be a limiting macronutrient of vegetation in the bogs, not N.

Input of inorganic N by deposition may have different implications on plant communities and plant traits than organic N input by N₂ fixation (van der Heijden et al., 2000; Malmer et al., 2003). Sphagnum mosses absorb inorganic N from deposition very efficiently on the surface through the capitula up to about 1 g N m⁻² yr⁻¹. (Nordbakken et al., 2003; Fritz et al., 2014). Vascular plants additionally take up inorganic N via their root system and thus rely on N recycling by mineralization of plant litter or nonsymbiotic N₂ fixation. The vertical profile of natural \(^{15}\)N signatures underlines the distinct N nutrition of plants in the CP and SPH plots. Negative \(δ^{15}\)N signatures in the vegetation of the CP plots indicate uptake of mineralized N and preceding discrimination of the \(^{15}\)N isotope by fungi. The \(^{15}\)N isotopes enrich at underlying peat layers, and the \(^{15}\)N signature becomes more positive. The slightly negative \(^{15}\)N signature of \(-0.7\%\%\) at 0–10 cm depth suggests that N₂ fixation also plays an important role for cushion plants. The positive \(^{15}\)N signature of \(6.7\%\%\) at 0–10 cm depth in the SPH plots provides evidence that N₂ fixation and N deposition are the dominant N sources for Sphagnum and that N mineralization is negligible. However, Sphagnum also may exhibit negative \(δ^{15}\)N signatures when mineralized N is available (Broder et al., 2012). It is difficult to assess the origin of N in plants because N deposition, N₂ fixation, and N mineralization display main potential sources with varying isotopic signature. Overall, higher N concentrations and smaller C/N ratios underpin the strength of N acquisition in the CP plots compared to the SPH plots.

Besides the river plume, the onshore advection of nutrient rich North Brazilian Current water (Demaster and Pope 1996), and anticyclonic (warm core) and cyclonic (cold core) North Brazilian Current rings (Fratantoni and Richardson 2006) may have a marked impact on the hydrology and biological activity of the shelf and in offshore waters between the equator and 10°N. Previous studies of the nutrient systematics in the Amazon River and its plume have shown nitrogen to be the most limiting nutrient for algal growth in both shelf (Demaster and Pope 1996) and offshore waters (Cooley and Yager 2006; Cooley et al. 2007). The Amazon River carries high concentrations of silicate (14–150 µmol L⁻¹) and phosphate (0.6–0.8 µmol L⁻¹) but nitrate concentrations of 12–23 µmol L⁻¹ are low compared to other large rivers like the Pearl (Cai et al. 2004) or Mississippi Rivers (Dagg et al. 2004), where nitrate concentrations are typically higher than 75 µmol L⁻¹. Within the plume, this nutrient composition leads to strong N limitation of algal growth at the outer Amazon shelf (4–5°N) where silicate and phosphate concentrations remain high (Demaster and Pope 1996). Algal blooms are nevertheless present on the outer Amazon shelf during all seasons (summarized by Demaster and Pope 1996). The depletion of dissolved inorganic nitrogen we observed in the river plume (Fig. 3A) and the shoaling of the nitracline into surface waters at the ES stations (Fig. 4A) are both consistent with an important role for advective inputs of nitrate-rich subplume waters in supporting primary production on the shelf. The elevated ammonium concentrations we found throughout the water column at MH1 and MH2 stations also suggest that regenerated nutrients make an 472

Our stations reflect a broad range of diazotrophic inputs to the N budget. For example, suspended particles at our MH2 and OC stations have generally low \( \delta^{15}N \) values, which are consistent with the higher N\(_2\) fixation rates we measured at these stations (Figs. 3-5). Particles at our ES stations have generally high \( \delta^{15}N \) values, in keeping with the lowest rates of N\(_2\) fixation we measured on this cruise. With the exception of Sta. 23, our MH1 stations fall between these two extremes, both in \( \delta^{15}N \) and in rates of N\(_2\) fixation. This overall pattern has been documented previously among oligotrophic (up to 100% diazotroph N in suspended particles) and more eutrophic (0–10% diazotroph N in suspended particles) areas in the Tropical North Atlantic (Montoya et al. 2002; Wannicke et al. 2010; Landrum et al. 2011) and the South China Sea (Loick et al. 2007).

In contrast to the relatively consistent isotopic systematics of our OC and ES stations, particles at stations with high abundances of DDAs and *Synechococcus* spp. showed wide variation in \( \delta^{15}N \), including high \( \delta^{15}N \) values above the nitracline (MH1 stations, Table 2). This pattern implies a significant input of sub-thermocline nitrate at stations where the *Hemiaulus/Richelia* association was present but not dominant (Goes et al. 2014) and where moderate to high N\(_2\) fixation rates occurred (MH 1 stations, Table 3). The sub-thermocline nitrate contribution was much lower at stations dominated by DDAs (MH2 stations, Table 4), which is consistent with previous observations of a very strong reliance on N\(_2\) fixation during a DDA bloom (Carpenter et al. 1999)

The low diazotroph contribution to PN above the nitracline at MH1 stations reflected the high abundance of symbiotic diatoms at these stations (Goes et al. 2014). The only MH1 station with high rates of N\(_2\) fixation was Sta. 23 (134 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1} \) in the >10 \( \mu \)m size fraction), which had a deep nitracline (100 m, Fig. 4), making significant inputs of sub-thermocline nitrate into surface waters unlikely. The sea surface salinity, silicate, and phosphate distributions at the MH1 stations were all similar to those of the ES stations (Table 2), which suggests an advective input of surface shelf water containing particles with a high \( \delta^{15}N \) signature derived from nitrate uptake on the shelf. The enhanced *Hemiaulus/Richelia* abundance (1927 cells L\(^{-1}\), Yeung et al. 2012) and high N\(_2\) fixation rates in the >10 \( \mu \)m size fraction at Sta. 23 indicate that DDAs were able to grow and fix N\(_2\) in the presence of nitrate, which is similar to the growth of DDAs in the Mekong plume (Grosse et al. 2010). We also found appreciable N\(_2\) fixation rates in the >10 \( \mu \)m size fraction at ES stations (Table 3) with elevated *Hemiaulus/Richelia* abundance (up to 744 cells L\(^{-1}\); R. A. Foster pers. comm.) and ambient DIN concentrations as high as 1–1.2 \( \mu \)mol L\(^{-1} \) (Stas. 4 and 16). These rates are similar to those found in the South China Sea off Vietnam (Voss et al. 2006). In this context, the frequency and intensity of nitrate injection into the mixed layer as well as the offshore advection from the shelf of seed populations of *Hemiaulus/Richelia* may all be critical aspects of the DDA niche in the Amazon Plume.

The movement of diazotroph N into the zooplankton community of the Amazon plume varied widely and reflected the diazotroph N contribution to PN. Generally small diazotroph contributions occurred at ES and MH1 stations (0–6%, excluding an outlier in zooplankton >5000 \( \mu \)m from Sta. 4), intermediate contributions occurred at OC stations (9–23%), and the highest diazotroph contribution was found at MH2 stations (21–45%, Table 4). This general pattern has been documented previously among oligotrophic (up to 65% diazotroph N in epipelagic zooplankton) and more eutrophic (0–10% diazotroph N in epipelagic zooplankton) areas in the Western and Eastern Tropical North Atlantic (Montoya et al. 2002; Wannicke et al. 2010; Landrum et al. 2011; Hauss et al. 2013).

Diazotroph nitrogen contributions were not evenly distributed among zooplankton size fractions. At all MH2 and most oceanic stations, diazotroph N contribution was highest in the smallest size fractions and generally decreased with zooplankton size (Table 4). In contrast, a number of stations (ES Sta. 4, MH1 Stas. 3 and 23, and OC Stas. 5 and 21) showed a different pattern in which the diazotroph contribution to total nitrogen was highest in the larger size fractions (> 1000 \( \mu \)m, Table 4). These two patterns corroborate earlier suggestions that diazotroph N may enter the food web either via the microbial loop (all MH2 and most oceanic stations) or via direct grazing (at ES Sta. 4, MH1 Stas. 3 and 23, and OC Stas. 5, 21, 27) by small as well as by larger zooplankton (Montoya et al. 2002; Mulholland 2007; Raes et al. 2014).

NGE of zooplankton in the different communities

We used a novel isotopic approach to constrain NGE in three different plankton communities. In contrast to the classical K\(_2\) approach, which is based on the difference in nitrogen: phosphorus ratios of the animal, its prey, and its excretion products (Le Borgne 1982 and references therein), our isotopic approach does not require incubation experiments.

The range of NGE values that we estimated for small mesozooplankton (43% to 76%, average 59 ± 10%, \( n = 19 \)) falls in the upper portion of the range of values derived from the K\(_2\) approach (18 to 71%) in the Eastern Tropical Atlantic and elsewhere (Le Borgne 1982 and references therein). Although we expected that direct grazing on diatoms and DDAs could result in more efficient nitrogen utilization, as suggested by Montoya et al. (2002) and Mulholland (2007), we found uniformly high NGEs for small mesozooplankton at all sites. Interestingly, this small range for NGEs compared to the results by Le Borgne (1982) occurred despite clear spatial differences in both food quantity (PN concentrations) and quality (C: N atomic ratios; Fig. 11).

but we can use the \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) of suspended particles as an integrative measure of the sources of nitrogen supporting production of biomass on the timescale of particle turnover, which is typically on the order of days to weeks (Montoya 2007; Landrum, Altabet, and Montoya 2011). Specifically, nitrogen stable isotope abundances provide a tool for assessing the relative contribution of diazotrophs to the pool of organic nitrogen in the upper water column.

We previously documented a clear relationship between the abundance of Amazon plume diazotrophs and the \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) of suspended particles at the sea surface (Weber et al. 2017), and here we extend this approach to the broader community as represented by the mass- and depth-weighted mean \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{PN} \) in the upper water column. The mean \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{PN} \) we found in the upper water column ranged from \( -2.9\% \) to \( +5.0\% \), spanning the range of values we used as isotopic end members for this system and suggesting that our choice of isotopic end members was appropriate for characterizing this system. Further, weighted mean \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{PN} \) values generally scaled inversely with areal rates of N-fixation across all habitat types we sampled (Fig. 6), implying that the instantaneous rates of activity we measured in our 24 h incubations are representative of timescales long enough to affect the bulk pool of suspended particles (days to weeks). In other words, N-fixation is not only widely distributed in the Amazon plume system, but also must have the spatial and temporal persistence to generate a measurable impact on the overall nitrogen budget of the upper water column.

Interestingly, the mean\( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) of particles showed a stronger dependence on the areal rate of N-fixation by small diazotrophs than on the activity of larger ones (Fig. 6). In both cases, we would expect the mean\( \delta^{15}\mathrm{PN} \) to asymptotically approach the\( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) of diazotroph nitrogen (i.e., \( -2\% \): Montoya, Carpenter, and Capone 2002) as N-fixation increases in importance as a source of new nitrogen supporting primary production. When plotted as a function of areal N-fixation by small diazotrophs (Fig. 6a), the mean \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) of suspended particles decreased very strongly from~\( 5\% \) to \( -2\% \) between the lowest rates measured and rates of \( \sim 100 \ \mu\mathrm{mol}\ \mathrm{m}^{-2}\ \mathrm{d}^{-1} \). In contrast, the mean \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) of particles showed a similar decline with large size fraction N-fixation rates up to about 150 \( \ \mu\mathrm{mol}\ \mathrm{m}^{-2}\ \mathrm{d}^{-1} \) (Fig. 6b). This difference suggests that nitrogen fixed by small cells enters the planktonic food web more efficiently than nitrogen fixed by larger cells, perhaps reflecting differences among the grazers feeding on different diazotrophs. This finding is complementary to our previous observations that DDAs have a much stronger impact on the food web and on vertical export than does *Trichodesmium* (Weber et al. 2017) and suggests that the overall coupling between N-fixation and the rest of the planktonic food web is tightest for small particles, intermediate for DDAs, and lowest for *Trichodesmium*.

Our water column mean\( \delta^{15}\mathrm{PN} \) can be recast into an estimate of the fraction of the standing stock of particulate organic nitrogen that is derived from recent N-fixation (\( \%N_{\mathrm{diaz}} \)) using a simple mixing model (Fig. 7a). Variations in \( \%N_{\mathrm{diaz}} \) reflect the overall contribution of N-fixation to the base of the food web, and we found \( \%N_{\mathrm{diaz}} \) values that ranged from near zero at YPC stations to about 100% at OSW stations, with intermediate values at OPC and plume margin (WPM and EPM) stations. 3. Results

a. Hydrographic properties and habitat types

As described by Weber et al. (2017), plume thickness and width varied along our cruise track, with the greatest extent toward the northern portion of our study area. We found substantial variation in the distribution of hydrographic properties on timescales of hours to days, reflecting the highly dynamic interactions between the plume and its surrounding waters. Of the major nutrients, only silicate showed a classic pattern of variation with salinity, while nitrate concentrations were low or below the limit of detection throughout our study region and phosphate concentrations varied widely, with many positive deviations from conservative mixing (Weber et al. 2017). Interestingly, the positive phosphate anomalies tended to increase with distance down the plume axis (fig. 2 of Weber et al. 2017), consistent with release of phosphate into the water column as the plume waters aged and interacted with the surrounding oceanic waters.

We categorized our stations using the five habitat types defined by Weber et al. (2019), which have already proved useful in delineating phytoplankton assemblages in this system. The five habitat types for this system form a sequence extending from the plume proper (YPC and OPC) to regions where the plume interacts with surrounding oceanic waters (OSW) at the western (WPM) and eastern (EPM) sides of the plume axis. The five habitat types are spatially intermingled to some extent (Fig. 1b), reflecting the dynamic nature of the plume and its surroundings.

b. Rates of N- and C-fixation

We found measurable rates of N- and C-fixation throughout our study region with clear vertical structure and marked variation among stations (Fig. 2, Table 1). In general, volumetric N-fixation rates (range: 0–0.55 nmol L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\), N = 123) were highest near the surface and decreased with depth, though the depth interval with elevated N-fixation rates differed among habitat types. The strongest depth stratification was associated with the WPM stations, while the EPM and OSW stations tended to show elevated rates over a greater depth range. Nitrogen Fixation in Seagrass Communities during Summer in the Gulf of Carpentaria, Australia

D. J. W. MoriartyA and M. J. O'DonohueB

A CSIRO Marine Laboratories, PO Box 120, Cleveland, Qld 4163, Australia.
B Department of Microbiology, University of Queensland, St Lucia, Qld 4067, Australia.

Abstract
Rates of acetylene reduction in seagrass communities in the Gulf of Carpentaria were determined in intact cores of sediment and seagrass and in slurries. Short-term incubations and three different methods were used to ensure that results could be reliably converted to rates of nitrogen fixation. At Groote Eylandt, values ranged from 16 to 47 mg N m^{-2} day^{-1} in a Syringodium isoetifolium community and from 13 to 19 mg N m^{-2} day^{-1} on a reef flat with Thalassia hemprichii. At Weipa, mean rates of nitrogen fixation were 25 mg N m^{-2} day^{-1} in an Enhalus acoroides community and 20 mg N m^{-2} day^{-1} on a mud bank below mangroves. About 5% of fixation was due to epiphytes on the seagrass leaves, and 8% of fixation associated with the Syringodium isoetifolium community occurred in washed roots and rhizomes; the remainder was due mostly to bacteria in the sediment. Nitrogen fixation supplied 8 to 16% of the nitrogen requirements of the plants.

Introduction
Seagrasses are significant components of the coastal flora of the Gulf of Carpentaria, Australia, and are essential to the survival of a commercial fishery for penaeid prawns (Staples et al. 1985; Poiner et al. 1987). There is a marked seasonal variation in seagrass and bacterial productivity in the tropical seagrass communities, with very high values, 4 to 9 g C m^{-2} day^{-1}, being found in summer (Moriarty et al. 1990; Pollard and Moriarty 1991). To sustain high growth rates, the seagrasses require large amounts of inorganic nitrogen and phosphorus (Patriquin 1972). The concentrations of inorganic nitrogenous nutrients, particularly ammonia, in interstitial water in seagrass beds may not be sufficient to meet the short-term growth requirements of the seagrass (Patriquin 1972; Moriarty et al. 1985). Therefore, nitrogen fixation may be an important process that influences primary production in these tropical seagrass beds, but rates of fixation have not been measured previously in the Gulf of Carpentaria. Nitrogen fixation by microorganisms may occur in the phyllosphere and rhizosphere of seagrasses (Patriquin and Knowles 1972; Oremland et al. 1976; Capone and Taylor 1977; Capone et al. 1979; Capone and Budin 1982; Smith and Hayasaka 1982a, 1982b; O'Donohue et al. 1991a, 1991b).

Acetylene reduction is a common method of estimating nitrogenase activity in seagrass beds, but as acetylene is not the natural substrate of nitrogenase, care is needed in the interpretation of results. Factors that affect the accuracy of results when acetylene reduction techniques are used, such as the speed at which acetylene diffuses to the nitrogen fixation sites, disturbance of relationships between bacteria, plants and sediments, and long time periods for analyses, have been overcome in sandy sediments with the use of intact cores and the perfusion technique described by O'Donohue et al. (1991a).

Nitrogen Fixation in Seagrass Communities 119 *Acetylene Reduction* At Groote Eylandt, rates of acetylene reduction were measured in intact cores of seagrass sediment by two different techniques. Firstly, the sediment was perfused with sea water containing acetylene (20% v/v). Secondly, sea water containing acetylene was placed in a chamber over the core of seagrass and the acetylene allowed to diffuse through the seagrass lacunae to the rhizosphere. For determination of acetylene and ethylene concentrations, 400 µL samples of sediment interstitial water and the associated water column were collected from intact cores at intervals of 2, 4 and 6h after perfusion was complete. Owing to the slow rate of percolation in the perfusion experiments, samples were not collected until 3 h after perfusion of the sediments had begun, in order to allow acetylene to permeate the sediments. With a needle and syringe, the interstitial water was collected through sampling ports in the side of the PVC pipe at 2-cm intervals. The methods are described in detail by O'Donohue et al. (1991a). Acetylene reduction in sediment, rinsed roots and rhizomes, and leaves was also measured in glass jars. For sediment and leaf samples, material was placed in 554-mL glass jars and the jars filled with sea water through which acetylene had been bubbled. Samples of the water were collected over time through a septum in the lid (O'Donohue et al. 1991a). Acetylene reduction at all Weipa sites was determined by this slurry technique. Because of the large size and robust nature of the *Enhalus* roots and rhizomes, sediment was collected between the plants within the bed. The cores and jars were incubated in daylight in bins of sea water. All water samples were stored in 5-mL vacuum containers with a small amount of acetic acid to stop acetylene reduction. The samples were analysed for acetylene and ethylene as previously described, and the theoretical ratio of 3 mol acetylene reduced:1 mol dinitrogen fixed was used to calculate rates of nitrogen fixation. Rates of acetylene reduction were determined by linear regression of ethylene concentration over time (O'Donohue et al. 1991a). The leaf and root and rhizome material from some experiments was freeze-dried and weighed. Analyses of variance were used to test for differences in rates between each community and for differences in rates at depths of 2 and 6 cm within each community. *Epiphytic Cyanobacteria* Fragments of the leaves of the seagrass used in the acetylene reduction analyses were examined for epiphytic cover by fluorescence microscopy (Moriarty 1980). **Results** Rates of nitrogen fixation in the open-bay community at Groote Eylandt were high, with values ranging from 16 to 47 mg N m$^{-2}$ day$^{-1}$. Mean values of 33 to 41 mg N m$^{-2}$ day$^{-1}$, determined by the perfusion and slurry methods, were not significantly different (Table 1). Discussion The high rates of nitrogen fixation recorded here for tropical seagrass communities are comparable to rates recorded for *Thalassia testudinum* beds in Barbados and the Bahamas (Table 4). Our experiments were undertaken in summer, when rates of primary and bacterial production are about five times greater than those in winter (Moriarty et al. 1990). We would expect that rates of nitrogen fixation in winter would also be lower because bacterial productivity is a measure of organic-carbon flux through heterotrophic bacteria and thus indicates the potential availability of carbon substrates for nitrogen fixation. The rates of nitrogen fixation in these seagrass communities are much greater than the rates of 1 to 4 mg N m⁻² day⁻¹ reported for mangrove communities in northern Queensland (Boto and Robertson 1990). The high rates of nitrogen fixation, which are similar to those reported for crops of legumes (Table 4), indicate that seagrasses may well be very significant sources of nitrogen for coastal communities in tropical regions. This was suggested by Patriquin and Knowles (1972), but others have not found such high values. The accuracy of values for rates of nitrogen fixation in seagrass beds that have been determined from rates of acetylene reduction has been questioned by Capone (1988), who recommends very short time periods for incubation with acetylene. The values reported by Patriquin and Knowles (1972) may be overestimates because they incubated slurries of sediment in small flasks for three to five days, during which time nitrogen fixation could have been simulated. The validity of the acetylene reduction methods that we used is supported by ¹⁵N studies (O'Donohue et al. 1991a, 1991b). The rates of acetylene reduction

This, together with the fact that they were obtained after short-term incubations (6–9 h) and that good agreement in rates of fixation for the top 4 cm was obtained by means of the perfusion and lacunal diffusion techniques, indicates that the values reflect actual rates of nitrogen fixation *in situ*. By providing a water column above the intact cores and sampling the sediment interstitial water and water column for acetylene and ethylene, we avoided problems due to disproportionate partitioning of acetylene and ethylene into liquid and gas phases (O'Donohue *et al.* 1991a). However, we found much greater variability in the regression of ethylene concentrations over time than the *r* values of 0.9 or better that have been reported for subtropical sandy sediments with mud contents of approximately 5% (O'Donohue *et al.* 1991a). The sample variability could result from the nonuniform distribution of the nitrogen-fixing bacteria at each depth or from the clay preventing even distribution of acetylene throughout the cores. The greater resistance to flow seen in the long perfusion times required (3 h) increases the likelihood that channelling occurred. Consequently, the interstitial-water samples may have been collected from areas where acetylene was not in saturating concentrations. With the slow rates of percolation in muddy sediments and the potential for uneven distribution of acetylene in the perfusion technique, the lacunal diffusion method appears to be an attractive means of providing saturating concentrations of acetylene to the potential nitrogen-fixing bacteria around the roots and rhizomes. Caution must be exercised, however, as the decrease in root and rhizome biomass with depth (Table 2) results in an uneven and probably nonsaturating concentration of acetylene below 4 cm. Diffusion of acetylene away from the root and rhizome surface is limited by the clay, so extrapolation of rates below 4 cm would underestimate potential nitrogen fixation (O'Donohue *et al.* 1991a). Hence, we did not calculate rates of nitrogen fixation below this depth for the lacunal diffusion results. Collecting more samples from each zone would give a better understanding of the variability in acetylene reduction at these depths. The cores should be shaken at the end of the incubation to evenly distribute ethylene throughout the water phase. The water phase should then be sampled and the total water volume measured to determine the total amount of ethylene produced over the incubation period.

In the open-bay and reef-flat communities, most nitrogen fixation occurred in the rhizosphere (Fig. 2). Of the ¹⁵N fixed in the rhizosphere of *Zostera capricorni* in Moreton Bay, Queensland, 57% was found in the leaves and roots within 6 h (O'Donohue et al. 1991b). Patriquin and Knowles (1972) and Capone and Taylor (1980) concluded that a substantial proportion of the nitrogen needed by *Thalassia testudinum* in the Caribbean was supplied by nitrogen fixation in the rhizosphere. Bacterial productivities, determined from rates of tritiated thymidine incorporation into DNA, were generally between 3 and 5 g C m⁻² day⁻¹ in these sediments in summer (Moriarty et al. 1990). There was an exceptionally high rate of production at the open-bay site at the time that the present nitrogen fixation measurements were made, but other values were similar to those obtained in a previous study (Table 5). The flux of organic carbon through the heterotrophic bacteria would be equal to the productivity if the growth efficiency was 50% and about twice the productivity if the growth efficiency was 30% (Moriarty 1989). Thus, the bacterial productivities give an upper limit for the availability of energy substrates for the nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Our data indicate that from 3 to 6 mg of nitrogen is fixed per gram of carbon oxidized by the heterotrophic bacteria if the average growth efficiency was 30% (Table 5). The efficiency with which aerobic bacteria fix nitrogen in culture ranges from 25 to 200 mg N g⁻¹ C (Döbereiner and Pedrosa 1987). Thus, the rates of nitrogen fixation in these seagrass beds could easily be sustained by the rates of organic-matter oxidation by bacteria and supply by primary producers. Rates of bacterial productivity measured concurrently by Pollard and Moriarty (1991 figs 2 and 6a) showed similar trends to the rates of nitrogen fixation reported here (Fig. 2).

Interestingly, these rates are of the same magnitude as seen in cyanobacterial mats found in temperate, sub-tropical, and tropical shallow marine systems such as coral reefs (Charpy et al., 2010) and intertidal lagoons (Steppe & Paerl, 2005). While cyanobacterial mats from warmer climates are composed of different species, the similarity of these rates indicates that temperature may be a driving factor in defining species composition, but not setting the areal N₂ fixation rates possible in these mats. As typically found in other terrestrial habitats (Izquierdo & Nüsslein, 2006; Zehr et al., 2003a, b), a large diversity of nifH sequences was observed. Shannon diversity index values ranged between 1.8 and 2.6 (Table 3), comparable with soils of the Arctic tundra (1.97), glacier fore-field (2.16–2.46) and tropical forest soil (2.41; Izquierdo & Nüsslein, 2006; Duc et al., 2009). Unexpectedly, cyanobacterial nifH phylotypes did not dominate the gDNA clone libraries; phylotypes from within the cyanobacteria, but also the alpha-, gamma-, delta-proteobacteria, and a clade most closely related to the beta-proteobacteria were all represented. These results mirror results from in marine-associated microbial mats and rice roots, whereby a large diversity of heterotrophic nifH genes have also been found to dominate nifH clone libraries (Ueda et al., 1995; Zehr et al., 1995; Steppe & Paerl, 2002). Low sequence homology (approximately < 90%) of the heterotrophic nifH sequences to their closest NCBI GenBank matches also indicates that they currently remain uncharacterized. Although cyanobacteria did not dominate the gDNA libraries, they were the most abundant phylotype (approximately 10⁵–10⁷ gene copies g⁻¹ soil) in the wetted soils and were the only phylotypes detected by qPCR in the cDNA fractions for both the Miers Valley transects: ML1-2 and MS1-3. However, it is important to note that the presence of nifH mRNA transcripts may not represent definitive N₂ fixation activity as nitrogenase is subject to posttranslational control (Steppe & Paerl, 2002). Also, some cDNA sequences were not retrieved from gDNA clone libraries and may indicate biases in the PCR assays or low copy genes that are highly expressed, whereas gDNA clones not present in cDNA represent genes that were not transcribed at the time of sampling. Likewise, differences between qPCR and cDNA libraries may indicate biases owing to the contrasting PCR conditions, for example, primers and annealing temperatures. © 2012 Federation of European Microbiological Societies Published by Blackwell Publishing Ltd. The ‘wet’ source samples (site 1) were also positive for N₂ fixation (0.7–2.0 nmol N cm⁻³ h⁻¹) with the exception of site 1 of the MS transect, which was collected in the center of the stream where high flow rates presumably inhibited the formation of a stable microbial community. Owing to the discovery of sulfate-reducing N₂ fixers from samples collected during the initial January 2009 sampling season, wetted DV soils were measured for N₂ fixation activities that were linked with sulfate reduction during the second, December 2009 sampling expedition. Through the inhibition of sulfate reduction by the addition of NaMoO₄, it was found that sulfate-dependent N₂ fixation activity accounted for a large proportion of the total N₂ fixation activities detected within wetted DV sites (Fig. 3). For example, approximately 50% of total N₂ fixation activities for both wetted transect sites, ML1-2 and MS1-3, were linked with sulfate reduction with rates decreasing from approximately 2.7 to 1.4 nmol N cm⁻² h⁻¹.

nifH gene analyses

The nifH gene was not initially detected by PCR in the ‘dry’ (site 4) soil samples with the exception of BL4, suggesting low gene copy numbers. However, an increase from 21 to 30 PCR cycles during the initial amplification resulted in detectable nifH amplicons. The nifH gene could not be detected by PCR in samples from the high flow rate Miers Stream (MS1-1) site. nifH-based T-RFLP analyses (method by Hewson & Fuhrman, 2006) were undertaken on all transect sites; however, owing to both low numbers of nifH TRFs (between 2 to 10) and single T-RFs for MS1-4 and ML1-3 (results not shown), results were not analyzed further. nifH clone libraries were constructed from the sampling sites with the highest detected N₂ fixation rates from each transect, that is, BL2, NP2, MS1-3, and ML1-2 (Table 3), and the cDNA from ML1-2, as this was the only cDNA sample that provided positive nifH PCR amplification (Table 3). Rarefaction curves of nifH libraries (Fig. S1) indicate that ML1-2 cDNA has reached its diversity plateau with slopes beginning to plateau for MS1-3 and ML1-2 and steep rarefaction curves for NP2 and BL2, signifying that the diversity of nifH in these sites are under-represented. Shannon diversity indices (at 95% sequence similarity) ranged between 1.8 and 2.6 for each individual nifH library (Table 3).

Four major nifH clusters were observed (Fig. 4) including two clades (group 1 and 2) within the delta-proteobacteria (one of which grouped closely with Geobacter sp.), one cluster within the cyanobacteria, and a group most closely related to the beta-proteobacteria. nifH phylotypes were also represented within the alpha- and gamma-proteobacteria. Table 3 includes the percentages of each phylotype detected within the samples. The MS1-3 and BL2 clone libraries were dominated by delta-proteobacterial-related signatures. Cyanobacterial phylotypes were most well represented in ML1-2, but not detected in BL2. ML1-2 cDNA contained a total of 6 OTUs that were dominated by cyanobacterial-related signatures and a single delta-proteobacterial OTU (OTU23) as opposed to 16 OTUs in DNA from the same site (at 95% sequence similarity). In total, only 3 of the 6 OTUs of the ML1-2 cDNA library were detected in the ML1-2 DNA library. Similarities of nifH phylotypes between sites were typically below approximately 56% with the exception of MS1-3 and ML1-2 sharing approximately 78% of their collective phylotypes (Table S2).

The majority of the nifH sequences showed low sequence similarity to nifH sequences within the NCBI GenBank database with sequence homologies typically not exceeding 90%. Higher sequence similarities (> 90%) were typically only obtained for nifH sequences related to cyanobacterial signatures previously recovered from the ice cover of Lake Bonney, Antarctica (Olson et al., 1998), and those most closely related to clones (OraP15 and OraP17) were recovered from microbial mat communities of a meltwater pool on the McMurdo ice shelf (Jungblut & Neilan, 2010).

Nitrogen-stimulated CO2 fixation was also evident in the RCNERR mats, but high variability among triplicates tended to obscure statistical significances between treatments and controls. Generally, maximum N stimulation occurred during the spring and fall periods (Tables 1 & 2). In North Carolina coastal waters, this pattern coincides with periods of most profound N limitation (Paerl et al. 1990, Rudek et al. 1991). Although examined over fewer intervals (quarterly), results from the Tomales Bay mats generally concur with the North Carolina findings. The addition of NO3− significantly (p < 0.05; 1-way ANOVA) stimulated CO2 fixation in approximately 20% of both the Lagunitas and Walker Creek samples. NO3− plus PO43− significantly stimulated 33% of the Walker Creek samples. In Tomales Bay, maximum N stimulation of mat CO2 fixation coincides with minimum water column DIN concentrations (S. V. Smith & J. T. Hollibaugh pers. comm.). In all mat systems, stimulation of microalgal production is rapid (within 24 h) and maintained as long as N enrichment continues, in support of longer-term enrichment experiments (Van Raalte et al. 1976). It would therefore appear that in a large number of cases, mat systems are poised to rapidly respond to N enrichment pulses, an observation shared with other N assimilatory and dissimilatory transformation (NO3− reduction, denitrification, nitrification) studies (Joye & Paerl 1993a, b). Nutrient impacts on mat N2 fixation The general observation of N-stimulated mat primary production, together with observed rapid production responses to N enrichment, suggests that potential sources of biologically available 'new' N are both in high demand and readily utilized to support primary production. In this regard, factors controlling 'new' N input, namely N2 fixation, may be of considerable importance in mediating mat production. To varying degrees, all mat systems exhibited N2 fixation; this process contributes significant amounts of 'new' N (ranging from 10 to nearly 100% of mat primary production N demands) (Bebout 1992, Joye & Paerl 1993a, b). By far, the most important and consistent nutrient controlling N2 fixation (nitrogenase activity, NA) in bioassays was DOC, supplied as either glucose, maltose or mannitol (Table 4, Figs. 1 & 2). In previous work on diverse North Carolina mats, other sugars (sucrose, mannose, xylose, galactose) and organic acids (acetate, malate, lactate) elicited stimulation of NA, although the magnitude of stimulation varied with the amount of C added (Paerl & Prufert 1987). Stimulation of NA by DOC was most profound, persistent (seasonally) and significant (p < 0.05) in Tomales Bay (Table 4). The RCNERR and SB mats also exhibited DOC stimulation (Fig. 1). The slower-growing Guerrero Negro and Storrs Lake mats showed less profound stimulation by DOC additions (Fig. 2). As with CO2 fixation studies, the relatively slow growth rates of these mat types prevented clear-cut observations of nutrient stimulation of NA. Added to this was the problem of high variability among triplicates. This variability was in large part attributable to the heterogeneity of mats (particularly stromatolitic mats, which were highly convoluted). It should also be pointed out that the Storrs Lake littoral mats were dominated by a heterocystous cyanobacterium (Scytonema spp.), in contrast to all other mats, in which non-heterocystous genera prevailed. Previous work has indicated that DOC stimulation of NA is more prevalent in mats dominated by non-heterocystous cyanobacteria (Paerl et al. 1987, Paulsen et al. 1991). The likely reason for this differential effect is that non-heterocystous cyanobacterial N2 fixation is more sensitive to O2 inactivation than it is among heterocystous cyanobacteria. Nitrogen fixation, ammonium and nitrate uptake during a bloom of Cylindrospermopsis raciborskii in Lake Balaton

Mátyás Présing¹, Sándor Herodek¹, Lajos Vörös¹ and István Kóbor²

With 4 figures and 2 tables in the text

Abstract: N₂-fixation and \(^{15}\)N-labelled ammonium and nitrate uptake were measured during a bloom of C. raciborskii in two basins of Lake Balaton. In the eastern basin when the chlorophyll-a content reached 70 \( \mu \)g/l the N₂-fixation was low (59 mg N m⁻² day⁻¹) and the N uptake was dominated by ammonium (393 mg N m⁻² day⁻¹). The nitrate uptake was of minor importance in both basins (43 and 55 mg N m⁻² day⁻¹, respectively). In the western basin, the chlorophyll-a content was 160 \( \mu \)g/l and recirculation of regenerated forms of nitrogen could not support the demand. Although the ammonium uptake was high (357 mg N m⁻² day⁻¹), the fixed nitrogen (407 mg N m⁻² day⁻¹) exceeded it. The daily integrated carbon and nitrogen uptake ratios were 5.2 (weight/weight) in both basins.

Introduction

Lake Balaton has a surface area of 594 km² and a mean depth of 3.2 m. The lake is visited by 2 million tourists in summer, but its water quality is threatened by eutrophication (Herodek 1984). The largest water blooms have been caused by the cyanobacterium Cylindrospermopsis raciborskii (Wołosz.) Seenaya and Subba Raju. It is a toxin producing species known from the tropical (Hawkins et al. 1985), subtropical (Branco & Senna 1994), and temperate waters (Jeeji-Bai et al. 1977 and Hindák 1988). This filamentous cyanobacterium appeared in the lake in 1978, and has gradually become dominant in the late summer plankton (Vörös et al. 1983, Gorzó & Kiss 1984, Padisák et al. 1984).

The concentrations of soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP) were very low (0–4 µg/l) during the entire year. Nitrogen fixation by the phytoplankton became measurable at the beginning of June in both basins (Table 2). In July and August it was insignificant in the eastern basin, but 2 orders of magnitude higher in the western one. The highest N2-fixation was observed at the beginning of September in the eastern (58.5 mg N m-2 day-1) and four weeks earlier in the western basin (406.8 mg N m-2 day-1). Although rates of primary production increased sooner than nitrogen fixation, their optima coincided. At the time of the uptake experiments, the ammonium and nitrate content of the water were 1.0 µg NH4-N/l and 1.1 µg NO3-N/l in the eastern and 2.6 µg NH4-N/l and 0.2 µg NO3-N/l in the western basin. The actual uptake velocities of ammonium calculated by the Michaelis-Menten equation were similar in the two basins, (7.7 µg N l-1 h-1 in the eastern and 7.0 µg N l-1 h-1 in the western), with the maximum uptake velocities four fold higher in the western (80 µg N l-1 h-1) than in the eastern (20 µg N l-1 h-1) one. Nitrate uptake values were much lower (v and Vmax) than values for ammonium uptake. There was no significant difference between the actual velocities measured in the eastern (1.1 µg N l-1 h-1) and in the western (1.4 µg N l-1 h-1) basins, but the maximal uptake velocity in the latter (17.5 µg N l-1 h-1) exceeded the value estimated for the eastern part (4.8 µg N l-1 h-1). The calculated daily uptake of ammonium and nitrate in the eastern basin were 392.7 mg N m-2 day-1 and 42.9 mg N m-2 day-1, respectively. The majority of nitrogen uptake at the peak of the C. raciborskii bloom originated from ammonium. The sum of the ammonium and nitrate taken up from the water (435.6 mg N m-2 day-1) and nitrogen fixation (58.5 mg N m-2 day-1) was 494.1 mg N m-2 day-1 (Fig. 4). Comparison with simultaneous carbon uptake (2.58 g C m-2 day-1) measured at the same time, showed a C/N ratio (weight/weight) of 5.2. Ammonium and nitrate uptake in the western basin were similar to those in the eastern one, 357 and 54.6 mg N m-2 day-1 ammonium and nitrate, respectively, but in the western basin the nitrogen fixation was much higher (406.8 mg N m-2 day-1) (Fig. 4) and constituted almost half of the total nitrogen utilization (818.4 mg N m-2 day-1). The ratio of the carbon (4341 mg C m-2 day-1) and total nitrogen uptake was similar (5.3 weight/weight) to that in the other part of the lake.
